title: How do you map a two-table parent-child relationship with @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @JoinColumn and mappedBy, and what does each annotation control?
topicTitle: How do you map a two-table parent-child relationship with @OneToMany

s1_definition.profdef: In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is an OWNING side and an INVERSE side. The child entity (the MANY side) holds `@ManyToOne` plus `@JoinColumn(name = "account_id")`; this is the OWNING side because the child table physically holds the foreign-key column. The parent entity (the ONE side) holds `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")`; `mappedBy` points at the FIELD NAME on the child that owns the relationship, marking the parent as the INVERSE (non-owning) side. The owning side is what Hibernate reads to decide what to write into the foreign-key column, so you must keep both sides in sync in Java by using helper methods. `@JoinColumn` names the actual FK column; `mappedBy` says "I am not the owner, the foreign key lives over there."
s1_definition.analogy: An account at National Bank of India has many trades. The trades table is where the `account_id` stamp physically lives on each row, so a trade "owns" the link and carries the `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(account_id)`. The account only "knows about" its trades through `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")` — it is the inverse side, like a customer file that references its receipts but where the actual account number is printed on each receipt, not the other way round.
s1_definition.oneliner: The MANY side with `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn` owns the foreign key; the ONE side with `@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)` is the inverse, and `mappedBy` names the owning field on the child, not a column.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is an OWNING side and an INVERSE side. The child entity (the MANY side) holds `@ManyToOne` plus `@JoinColumn(name = "account_id")`; this is the OWNING side because the child table physically holds the foreign-key column. The parent entity (the ONE side) holds `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")`; `mappedBy` points at the FIELD NAME on the child that owns the relationship, marking the parent as the INVERSE (non-owning) side. The owning side is what Hibernate reads to decide what to write into the foreign-key column, so you must keep both sides in sync in Java by using helper methods. `@JoinColumn` names the actual FK column; `mappedBy` says "I am not the owner, the foreign key lives over there."

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An account at National Bank of India has many trades. The trades table is where the `account_id` stamp physically lives on each row, so a trade "owns" the link and carries the `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(account_id)`. The account only "knows about" its trades through `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")` — it is the inverse side, like a customer file that references its receipts but where the actual account number is printed on each receipt, not the other way round.

**One line to remember:** The MANY side with `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn` owns the foreign key; the ONE side with `@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)` is the inverse, and `mappedBy` names the owning field on the child, not a column.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the exact problem we hit at National Bank of India when we first modelled accounts and their trades.

Problem 1 — trades being written with a NULL account. A developer added trades to `account.getTrades()` and called save, but every new row landed with `account_id = NULL`. The screen then showed orphan trades that belonged to no account. This is exactly how the owning side works: the `@OneToMany` collection on the account is the inverse side and does not drive the foreign-key column, so unless the child's `account` field is set, Hibernate has nothing to write into `account_id`. The fix was a synchronisation helper that sets both sides.

Problem 2 — every account lookup dragging in trades we did not want. Because `@ManyToOne` defaults to EAGER on the child, listing trades also eagerly loaded each account, and in some flows the reverse over-fetch happened too. This is exactly where overriding to `FetchType.LAZY` helps: associations load only when explicitly navigated.

Problem 3 — deleting a trade from an account not actually deleting it. Removing a trade from the collection left the database row in place because nothing cascaded. This is exactly where `orphanRemoval = true` helps: a trade removed from its account's collection is treated as an orphan and deleted.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a parent `Account` entity with `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account", cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true)` and `addTrade`/`removeTrade` helpers that keep both sides in sync. There is a child `Trade` entity with `@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "account_id")`. The `AccountRepository` exposes a `JOIN FETCH` finder so we can load an account with its trades in one query. The `TradingService`, annotated `@Transactional`, opens an account, adds two trades through the helper, saves the parent once, and relies on cascade to insert the children; a second method removes a trade and relies on orphan removal to delete it. The demo proves the foreign key is set correctly, that one save cascades to children, and that removal deletes the orphan row. A test checks the helper sets both sides.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is placing two trades on Rajesh's account `SAV2001`, then cancelling one.

Step 1: `placeTrades("SAV2001")` runs inside a `@Transactional` method, so a Hibernate session is open. It loads the managed `Account` for `SAV2001`.

Step 2: We create two transient `Trade` objects and call `account.addTrade(t1)` and `account.addTrade(t2)`. The helper adds each trade to the account's `trades` list (the inverse side, for navigation) AND sets `trade.setAccount(account)` (the owning side). This second step is what actually matters for the database, because the owning side is what Hibernate reads to fill `account_id`.

Step 3: We call `accountRepo.save(account)` once. Because the relationship has `cascade = CascadeType.ALL`, Hibernate also persists the two new trades. For each, it issues `INSERT INTO trades (trade_id, account_id, symbol, amount, status) VALUES (?, 'SAV2001', ?, ?, ?)`. The `account_id` is `SAV2001` precisely because the owning side was set in the helper — had we skipped that, it would be NULL.

Step 4: The cancel flow loads the account with its trades via `JOIN FETCH` (one query), finds `TRD-001`, and calls `account.removeTrade(trade)`. The helper removes it from the list and sets its `account` to null.

Step 5: On flush, `orphanRemoval = true` sees that `TRD-001` was removed from the owning account's collection and issues `DELETE FROM trades WHERE trade_id = 'TRD-001'`. The row is gone, not merely detached.

```
2026-10-24 00:33:02 INFO  TradingService - loaded Account SAV2001 (managed)
2026-10-24 00:33:02 FINE  TradingService - addTrade: set trade.account=SAV2001 (owning side)
2026-10-24 00:33:02 INFO  TradingService - save(account) → cascade INSERT trades(..., account_id='SAV2001') ×2
2026-10-24 00:33:02 INFO  TradingService - cancelTrade TRD-001 → orphanRemoval DELETE FROM trades WHERE trade_id='TRD-001'
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is always an owning side and an inverse side, and the distinction comes straight from the database: the foreign key is a single column on one table. For an account and its trades, the trades table holds the account_id column, so the Trade entity is the owning side and carries the ManyToOne annotation together with JoinColumn naming that foreign-key column. The Account entity is the inverse side and carries OneToMany with mappedBy, and the value of mappedBy is the name of the owning field on the Trade entity, not a column name. The inverse side never drives SQL on its own; Hibernate reads the foreign key only from the owning side.

The classic bug this causes is adding a child only to the parent's collection and forgetting to set the child's reference back to the parent, which leaves the foreign key null. I prevent that with synchronisation helper methods on the parent, like addTrade and removeTrade, that update both the collection and the child's owning reference in one call. In our account and trades model at National Bank of India, those helpers guarantee the account_id is always set, and because the relationship is configured with cascade all and orphan removal, saving the account once inserts all its new trades, and removing a trade from the collection deletes that row.

The production decisions I always make are to override the ManyToOne default from eager to lazy so I do not over-fetch the parent on every child read, to use a JOIN FETCH query when I genuinely need the account with its trades so I avoid the N plus one problem, and to apply cascade only to genuinely owned children. I would cascade from an account to its own trades, but I would never cascade a remove into shared reference data. The senior nuance I mention is that for set-based collections I base equals and hashCode on a stable business key like the trade id rather than the generated primary key, so an entity behaves correctly in the collection both before and after it is assigned a database id.
